To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cAMP and cGMP, when present in the absence of detergent, do not alter maximum Ca activated force in hyperpermeable cardiac muscle but that the addition of detergent to the bath causes a large increase in force that is inhibited by cGMP.
cAMP and cGMP regulate cardiac contractile proteins by phosphorylation and that this regulation is controlled through the beta receptor-adenylate cyclase system.
(1) The inotropic effect produced by cAMP and epinephrine in cardiac muscle involves a cAMP-regulatable phosphorylation that can control contractility in the absence of Ca regulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism by which cyclic nucleotides and guanine nucleotidetriphosphates regulate the contractility of mammalian cardiac muscle.
the regulation of the cardiac contractile proteins by cyclic nucleotides and the role of the sarcoplasmic Ca concentration in this process.
the mechanisms of cardiac muscle contraction and the role of cyclic nucleotides and guanine nucleotids in regulating the contractility.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cyclic nucleotides regulate contractility of cardiac muscle through the phosphorylation of a membrane protein that is controlled through the beta-adrenergic system.

cAMP, GTP, cGMP or epinephrin can regulate contractility by phosphorylation of a sarcolemmal protein, but that the regulation of contractility in cardiac muscle is not due to phosphorylation of myosin or troponin.

cAMP, GTP, epinephrine, and GMP-PNP can increase contractile force in rat cardiac muscle, but the mechanism of action for cAMP and epinephrine involves a phosphorylation reaction, and that for GTP and GMP-PNN is not phosphorylation but is dependent on the Ca sensitivity of contractility.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the contractile system is directly regulated by Ca, but Ca regulation is modulated by cAMP.

the inotropic response of cardiac muscle to cAMP is due to a phosphorylation of an unknown protein that is regulated through the beta-receptors and that the inotropic effect to guanine nucleotidase is a result of the direct interaction of these nucleotides with the contractile proteins.
the inotropic effects of cAMP, epinephrine, and GTP are not due to a change in the Ca sensitivity of cardiac muscle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inotropic effect is not due to a direct interaction of cAMP with troponin or myosin.
the contractile proteins of cardiac muscle can be directly regulated by cyclic nucleotides and guanine nucleotidetriphosphates.
the contractile system is a very complex system that has a lot of regulatory proteins that are involved in the regulation of the contractility.
